title: Valmiki's Poem: From Ayodhya to the Forest
bigQuestion: What does it mean to do what is right for your role?

story.title: Sandals on the Throne
story.kicker: A brother carries a pair of sandals home and sets them on an empty throne.
paragraphs: Prince Bharata walks slowly back into the city of Ayodhya. His eyes are red from crying. In his hands he carries something small. It is a pair of wooden sandals.
The sandals belong to his older brother, Rama. Rama has gone to live in the forest for fourteen years. Everyone says Bharata should be king now. The people wait to see what he will do.
Bharata climbs the steps to the great hall. He does not sit on the throne. Instead, he kneels down. Carefully, he places Rama's sandals on the seat. The hall is silent.
"These sandals will rule," he tells the court. "I will only take care of the kingdom for my brother. When Rama comes home, the throne is his." Then he bows to the sandals.
The people are quiet. Then some begin to cry too. They have never seen a prince turn down a crown. Many Hindus still tell this story as a picture of loyalty and doing what is right.
story.think: Bharata could have been king. Why do you think he put the sandals on the throne instead?

sections.title: The First Poet and His Poem

lessons.title: Valmiki, the First Poet
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu tradition honors Valmiki as the first poet and the author of the Ramayana.
reading: Hindu tradition calls *Valmiki* the adi kavi, which means "the first poet." Tradition says he made the Ramayana in Sanskrit. The poem tells the life of Prince Rama.
The poem itself tells how Valmiki began. He saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of birds. The other bird cried out in grief. Valmiki felt deep sorrow, and his words came out in a new rhythm.
Tradition says that rhythm became the shloka, the verse form of the whole poem. So, the story goes, poetry was born from sorrow and care for another living thing.

words.d: the sage whom Hindu tradition honors as the first poet and author of the Ramayana
a verse form with a steady rhythm, used in the Ramayana

look.title: Poetry Born From Grief
look.text: Valmiki sees a hunter kill one of two birds. Its mate cries out. Valmiki's sorrow pours out as a curse on the hunter, spoken in a new, even rhythm. He is surprised by his own words.
look.cite: Retold from Valmiki's Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Book 1), canto 2
look.prompt: What feeling does the poem say started Valmiki's poetry?

check.q: What does adi kavi mean?
check.why: Tradition calls Valmiki the adi kavi, the first poet.

check.q: What did Valmiki see before he spoke his first verse?
choices: A hunter shoot one of two birds
check.why: Bala Kanda tells of the hunter and the pair of birds.

check.q: What is a shloka?
choices: A verse form with a steady rhythm
check.why: The shloka is the verse form of the Ramayana.

lessons.title: Seven Books
lessons.mainIdea: Valmiki's Ramayana has seven books, called kandas, and about 24,000 verses.
reading: Valmiki's Ramayana is divided into seven books. Each book is called a *kanda*. Each kanda tells one part of Rama's life, from his childhood to the end of his reign.
The poem has about 24,000 verses, by the traditional count. That is very long. It would take many days to chant it all. Many families read a small part at a time.
The names of the books tell where the story happens. Ayodhya Kanda happens in Rama's city. Aranya Kanda happens in the forest. Sundara Kanda, the "beautiful book," follows Hanuman to Lanka.

words.d: one of the seven books of the Ramayana
a line or small group of lines in a poem

look.title: The Seven Kandas
look.cite: Valmiki's Ramayana; book names as in Griffith, The Ramayan of Valmiki (1870–74)
look.prompt: In which book does the battle happen?

check.q: What is a kanda?
choices: One of the seven books of the Ramayana
check.why: The Ramayana has seven books called kandas.

check.q: About how many verses does the Ramayana have?
check.why: The traditional count is about 24,000 verses.

check.q: Which kanda follows Hanuman to Lanka?
check.why: Sundara Kanda, the fifth book, follows Hanuman.

lessons.title: How Old Is the Ramayana?
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition and scholars give different dates for the Ramayana.
reading: Hindu tradition places Rama's life in a very ancient age of the world, called the Treta Yuga. Many Hindus believe Rama lived long, long ago, far earlier than written history.
Scholars look at the poem's language and its history. Most date Valmiki's poem to between about 500 BCE and 100 CE. Many think the first and last books were added later.
Both views are held today. A student can name both without choosing between them. You might say, "Tradition says..." and then, "Scholars date..." Both are part of learning.

words.d: beliefs and practices handed down over time
a person who studies a subject very carefully

look.title: Two Answers to One Question
look.text: A student asks, "How old is the Ramayana?" Her grandmother says Rama lived in a very ancient age. Her teacher says scholars date the poem to about 500 BCE to 100 CE. Both answers are shared with care.
look.prompt: How can you report both answers fairly in one sentence?

check.q: In which age does tradition place Rama?
check.why: Hindu tradition places Rama in the Treta Yuga.

check.q: How do most scholars date Valmiki's poem?
check.why: Most scholars date it between about 500 BCE and 100 CE.

check.q: What is a fair way to report both views?
choices: Say what tradition holds and what scholars date
Say only one view is allowed
check.why: A fair report names both the traditional view and the scholarly date.

lessons.title: A King and Four Sons
lessons.mainIdea: King Dasharatha of Ayodhya has four sons, and Rama is the eldest.
reading: The Ramayana begins in *Ayodhya*, a rich city in North India. Its king is Dasharatha. He is a good king, but for many years he has no children. He prays and waits.
At last, the poem says, his three queens have four sons. Queen Kausalya's son is Rama. Queen Kaikeyi's son is Bharata. Queen Sumitra has twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna.
Rama is the eldest. He grows up brave, kind and wise. He marries Sita, a princess from the kingdom of Mithila. The king plans to make Rama the next ruler.

words.d: Rama's home city in the Ramayana
the king of Ayodhya and Rama's father

check.q: Who is Rama's father?
check.why: Dasharatha, king of Ayodhya, is Rama's father.

check.q: Who is Bharata's mother?
check.why: Bharata is Kaikeyi's son.

check.q: Where is Sita from?
check.why: Sita is a princess of Mithila.

lessons.title: Kaikeyi's Two Wishes
lessons.mainIdea: Queen Kaikeyi uses two old promises to change who will be king.
reading: Long before, Queen Kaikeyi saved Dasharatha's life in a battle. He promised her two wishes, called boons. She could ask for them any time. He never forgot that promise.
Now Rama is about to be crowned. Kaikeyi's maid, Manthara, stirs up her fears. Kaikeyi goes to the king. She asks for her two boons at last. Manthara tells Kaikeyi her son will lose everything.
First, she wants her son Bharata to be king. Second, she wants Rama sent to the forest for fourteen years. The king is heartbroken. But he gave his word, and he cannot take it back.

words.d: a wish or gift promised to someone
being sent away from your home

look.title: A Hard Promise
look.text: Dasharatha loves Rama very much. He also gave his word to Kaikeyi long ago. If he breaks his promise, he is not a truthful king. If he keeps it, he loses his son.
look.prompt: What two good things are pulling against each other for the king?

check.q: Why did the king owe Kaikeyi two boons?
check.why: Kaikeyi saved Dasharatha in battle, and he promised her two boons.

check.q: What is a boon?
check.why: A boon is a wish someone has promised to grant.

check.q: What was Kaikeyi's second wish?
choices: Rama sent to the forest for fourteen years
check.why: She asked for Rama's exile for fourteen years.

lessons.title: Rama Chooses Exile
lessons.mainIdea: Rama accepts exile calmly so that his father's word is kept.
reading: Rama hears the news. He does not argue. He does not get angry. The poem shows him accepting the exile calmly, so that his father's promise is kept. He says he is ready to go.
Sita insists on coming with him. She says a wife's place is at her husband's side. Lakshmana insists on coming too, to serve and protect his brother. Neither one will stay behind.
The three leave Ayodhya in simple clothes made of bark. The people weep. Soon after, King Dasharatha dies of grief. Many readers see this as one of the saddest parts of the poem.

words.d: to agree to something, even if it is hard
deep sadness, especially after a loss

look.title: Rama's Answer
look.text: Rama tells Kaikeyi he is glad to go to the forest to keep his father's word. He says he would do even more to honor his father's promise.
look.cite: Retold from Valmiki's Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Book 2)
look.prompt: Why do you think the poem shows Rama as calm, not angry?

check.q: How does Rama react to the news?
check.why: Ayodhya Kanda shows Rama accepting exile calmly.

check.q: Who goes with Rama into exile?
check.why: Sita and Lakshmana choose to go with Rama.

check.q: What happens to King Dasharatha?
check.why: The poem says the king dies of grief after Rama leaves.

lessons.title: Bharata's Choice
lessons.mainIdea: Bharata refuses the throne and rules in Rama's name, with Rama's sandals on the throne.
reading: Bharata was away when all this happened. When he comes home, he is shocked. He does not want a crown won this way. He goes to the forest to bring Rama back.
Rama says no. He must keep his father's word. So Bharata asks for Rama's sandals. He carries them home and places them on the throne. Rama agrees and blesses him.
Bharata rules for fourteen years as Rama's stand-in. The poem says he lives simply, outside the city, waiting for his brother. Many Hindus honor Bharata as a model of a loyal brother.

words.d: staying true to someone or something
a person who takes someone's place for a while

look.title: What the Sandals Mean
look.text: A pair of sandals sits on a golden throne. No one sits there. Every day, Bharata makes decisions in Rama's name. The sandals remind everyone who the true king is.
look.prompt: What do the sandals stand for in this part of the story?

check.q: What does Bharata place on the throne?
check.why: Bharata places Rama's sandals on the throne.

check.q: Why does Bharata go to the forest?
check.why: Bharata wants Rama to come home and rule.

check.q: How do many Hindus see Bharata?
choices: As a model of a loyal brother
check.why: Many Hindus honor Bharata's loyalty to Rama.

lessons.title: Sages and Simple Living
lessons.mainIdea: In the forest, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana live simply and meet wise sages.
reading: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana walk deep into the forests of India. They build huts of leaves and branches. They eat fruit and roots. They live very simply.
In the forest, they meet many sages. A sage is a wise person who lives a holy life. The sages welcome them and teach them. Some ask Rama to protect them from danger.
The poem describes rivers, flowers, birds and changing seasons. Many readers love these nature scenes. Some of the places named in the poem are still pilgrimage sites today.

words.d: a wise person who lives a holy life
a journey to a holy place

look.title: A Day in the Forest
look.text: At dawn, Sita gathers flowers by the river. Lakshmana brings water and wood. Rama visits a sage who lives nearby. In the evening, they sit by a small fire and listen to the birds.
look.prompt: How is this life different from life in a palace?

check.q: What is a sage?
choices: A wise person who lives a holy life
check.why: Sages are wise people who live holy lives.

check.q: How do Rama, Sita and Lakshmana live in the forest?
check.why: They build simple huts and live on fruit and roots.

check.q: What is a pilgrimage?
choices: A journey to a holy place
check.why: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place.

lessons.title: Dharma: Right for Your Role
lessons.mainIdea: In the Ramayana, dharma means doing what is right for your role in life.
reading: The Ramayana is full of a key word: *dharma*. In this story, dharma means doing what is right for your role. A son, a brother, a wife and a king each have duties.
Rama keeps his father's word. Bharata protects his brother's throne. Lakshmana serves his brother. Sita stays true to Rama. Many Hindus see each one as a model of dharma.
Dharma is not always easy. Sometimes two duties pull against each other, like the king's love for his son and his promise. The Ramayana shows people facing these hard choices.

words.d: duty, or the right way to live for your role in life
something you should do because of your role

look.title: Four People, Four Duties
rows: Bharata guards the throne for Rama
look.prompt: Pick one person. What role is that person living up to?

check.q: What does dharma mean in the Ramayana?
choices: Doing what is right for your role
check.why: In the Ramayana, dharma means doing right for your role.

check.q: How does Rama show dharma?
choices: He takes the throne by force
check.why: Rama keeps his father's promise.

check.q: Why is dharma sometimes hard?

check.why: The poem shows duties that clash, like the king's love and his promise.

lessons.title: Tulsidas Tells It Again
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1500s, the poet Tulsidas retold the Ramayana in a form of Hindi.
reading: Valmiki's poem is in Sanskrit. Most people in North India did not speak Sanskrit. In the 1500s, the poet *Tulsidas* retold the story in Awadhi, a form of Hindi.
His poem is called the Ramcharitmanas, "the lake of Rama's deeds." Tulsidas was a devoted follower of Rama. His telling is full of love for Rama as God.
The Ramcharitmanas became one of the most loved books in North India. Families chant it at home and in temples. Many Hindus in Illinois know its verses by heart.

words.d: the poet who retold the Ramayana in a form of Hindi in the 1500s
full of love and loyalty

look.title: Two Tellings Side by Side
look.text: Valmiki tells Rama's story as a great epic about a noble prince. Tulsidas, many centuries later, tells it as a song of devotion to Rama as God. Both tell the same events. Each has its own feeling.
look.prompt: Why might a poet retell a story that people already know?

check.q: Who retold the Ramayana in a form of Hindi?
check.why: Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, a form of Hindi.

check.q: When did Tulsidas write?
check.why: Tulsidas wrote in the 1500s.

check.q: What feeling fills the Ramcharitmanas?
check.why: Tulsidas writes with deep devotion to Rama.
